newsitem.title: SENEGAL: World Bank head begins Africa tour.
newsitem.headline: World Bank head begins Africa tour.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn began a new African tour in Senegal on Saturday, saying he was keen to find ways to boost private investment in the continent.
Wolfensohn, who chose Africa for his first trip following his appointment in 1995, will also visit Ghana, Mozambique and South Africa during his nine-day trip.
"What is most needed is to find a way to bring in private investments in this country," he told reporters on arrival in the Senegalese capital, Dakar.
Before leaving Washington, he told a news conference that African nations were making real economic progress and said he wanted to build on that success.
"Africa is the World Bank's top priority and we want to strengthen our partnerships with the region," he said. "We've got money available. What we need are satisfactory projects."
Last year the World Bank approved $2.7 billion in loans for African countries covering 53 projects.
Wolfensohn, who in the past stressed rooting out corruption in developed and developing countries, made clear before leaving he would pull no punches on that issue.
"I will be as always very frank," he said. "Corruption is one of the greatest inhibitors to investors."

In Dakar, he paid tribute to Senegal's geographical location on West Africa's Atlantic coast, where it is the first major port of call for boats travelling south. "I am sure we will find a solution," he said of investment.
During his visit, he will inaugurate new offices in Senegal of the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank subsidiary that will fund activities of the private sector.
He was to hold talks with Senegalese President Abdou Diouf and the business community and to visit agricultural projects.

Before leaving Washington, Wolfensohn, who heads for Ghana on Monday, said the World Bank and other financial institutions were pressing ahead with a plan to provide debt relief to the world's poorest nations, many of them in Africa.
"It still looks like Uganda is likely to be the first subject of discussion," he added, noting this could be by end-April.
Speaking to reporters in London, British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke named Guyana, Burkina Faso and the Ivory Coast as other countries that might benefit from the debt relief plan.
